system: The City University of New York

leaders.priorTitle: Dean of the School of Liberal Arts
leaders.notes: Twelfth president of Hunter College, 1995 to 2000. Came from Purdue University, where he had been dean of the School of Liberal Arts for eight years and a faculty member since 1969. Left Hunter in 2000 to become the sixth president of Pace University, where he served until 2007.

leaders.priorTitle: Acting Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs
leaders.notes: Interim president July 2000 to June 2001, an internal promotion from Hunter's acting provost/senior VP for academic affairs (he had joined Hunter as VP for Administration in 1996). After the interim presidency he moved to Queens College as interim provost in 2001, became provost in 2003 until retiring in 2009, and later served as interim president of Queens College in spring 2014.

leaders.priorTitle: Chair, New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
leaders.priorInstitution: New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: The New York Stem Cell Foundation
leaders.notes: Thirteenth president, June 2001 to June 2023, one of the longest tenures in Hunter's history at 22 years; came directly from chairing the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission (1994 to 2001). She led Hunter's transformation into a selective, highly ranked college and raised more than $500 million. Her December 2022 announcement that she would step down was widely reported as sudden. In January 2024 she became president and CEO of The New York Stem Cell Foundation.

leaders.priorTitle: Dean Emerita, Macaulay Honors College (former University Professor, CUNY Graduate Center)
leaders.priorInstitution: The City University of New York
leaders.nextRole: Professor of Practice / Special Adviser to the President
leaders.notes: Interim president July 1, 2023 to August 2024, bridging Raab and Cantor. Dean emerita of CUNY's Macaulay Honors College, which she led 2006 to 2016, and previously a University Professor at the CUNY Graduate Center. After the interim term she continued as a professor of practice and special adviser to the president at Arizona State University and as a writer on higher education.

leaders.priorTitle: Chancellor
leaders.notes: Fourteenth president, took office August 12, 2024. Came from a decade as chancellor of Rutgers University-Newark (2014 to June 2023); earlier she was chancellor and president of Syracuse University and chancellor of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. A social psychologist, she is the daughter of a Hunter College alumna. Still sitting as of July 2026; no active presidential search.

leaders.priorTitle: Dean, College of Arts and Sciences
leaders.priorInstitution: North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University
leaders.notes: Eighth president, took office July 1, 1987 and served 16 years, the second-longest tenure in DSU history; his presidency spanned the 1993 elevation from Delaware State College to Delaware State University. Retired June 30, 2003 and died May 21, 2019 at age 81.

leaders.priorTitle: Fellow and Lecturer, Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, John F. Kennedy School of Government
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: University of the District of Columbia
leaders.notes: Ninth president, effective July 1, 2003; a Yale physics Ph.D. and former U.S. State Department diplomat who had been president of Queens College, CUNY (1995 to 2000) before his Harvard fellowship. Launched DSU's first doctoral programs but drew a 2005 no-confidence vote and low faculty-confidence survey; resigned August 30, 2008 to lead UDC, where he was later fired in 2012.

leaders.priorTitle: Chairman, Board of Trustees
leaders.nextRole: Returned as Chairman, Board of Trustees
leaders.notes: Acting president September 1, 2008 to January 9, 2010; a retired DuPont research chemist and longtime DSU board member who stepped aside from the board chairmanship to run the university during the search that produced Harry Williams. He resumed the chairmanship in 2010 and the campus administration building was named for him in 2015.

leaders.priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
leaders.notes: Internal promotion: sworn in as 10th president January 10, 2010 after 18 months as DSU provost; earlier held posts at the University of North Carolina General Administration, Appalachian State and North Carolina A&T. DSU rose sharply in HBCU rankings during his tenure; he left at the end of 2017 to lead the Thurgood Marshall College Fund and was named DSU president emeritus in 2021.

leaders.priorTitle: Chair, Board of Trustees
leaders.nextRole: Retirement; returned as member of the Board of Trustees
leaders.notes: Served as acting president January 2 to June 30, 2018 after Williams departed, then was elected 11th president by unanimous board vote effective July 1, 2018; the first woman to chair the DSU board and the first woman to lead the university. A four-decade higher-education administrator, she announced her retirement effective December 31, 2019 and rejoined the DSU board in January 2020.

leaders.priorTitle: Executive Vice President and Provost
leaders.notes: Internal promotion: became 12th president January 1, 2020 after joining DSU as provost in 2017 from Bank of America; earlier an executive VP at MBNA America and a speechwriter for then-Senator Joseph R. Biden Jr. Chaired the President's Board of Advisors on HBCUs from 2021 to January 2025 and was CEO of the 59th Presidential Inaugural Committee; oversaw the acquisition of Wesley College. Still sitting as of July 2026; no active presidential search found.

leaders.priorTitle: Director of Academic Affairs, corporate office
leaders.notes: Seventh president. Took office May 4, 1992 (initially as interim, made permanent by the Tennessee Board of Regents in 1993); ETSU's official list records his tenure as 1992 to 1996 without an interim designation. A veteran Tennessee higher-education and state-government figure who had been TBR chancellor 1975 to 1986. Retired December 31, 1996.

leaders.priorTitle: Vice President for Health Affairs and Dean, James H. Quillen College of Medicine
leaders.notes: Eighth president, an internal promotion: a board-certified vascular surgeon who came to ETSU in 1985 and rose from faculty to dean of the medical college to vice president for health affairs before the Tennessee Board of Regents named him president effective January 1, 1997. No interim separated him from Nicks. His 15-year tenure produced the Gatton College of Pharmacy, the Honors College and the Gray Fossil Site. He died March 5, 2026 at age 81.

leaders.priorTitle: Chancellor
leaders.priorInstitution: West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission
leaders.notes: Ninth president, an external hire who took office January 15, 2012 after five years leading West Virginia's statewide higher-education coordinating board. He led ETSU through the 2016 FOCUS Act transition to its own Board of Trustees in 2017, relaunched football, and oversaw the R2 Carnegie classification. The Board of Trustees approved a new five-year contract in November 2023; he remains in office as of July 2026 with no active presidential search.

leaders.priorTitle: Vice President for Academic Affairs
leaders.priorInstitution: East Texas State University (this same institution before its 1996 renaming)
leaders.nextRole: Retired; named President Emeritus; died December 11, 2008
leaders.notes: Ninth president, in office January 1, 1987 to late 1997; a career internal who joined the campus in 1970 and rose through dean of admissions, graduate dean and chief academic officer. He led the drive that took East Texas State University into The Texas A&M University System on September 1, 1996, triggering the rename to Texas A&M University-Commerce. He died of cancer December 11, 2008 at age 73.

leaders.priorTitle: Dean of Graduate Studies (1983 to 1997), then Interim President in early 1998
leaders.nextRole: Retired and returned to the faculty as Professor of History (President Emeritus)
leaders.notes: Tenth president; a pure internal promotion, a historian on the faculty since 1969 who was graduate dean 1983 to 1997, ran the university as interim in early 1998, and was named president and CEO in September 1998. He announced retirement in August 2007 effective July 31, 2008; the campus science building was named for him in 2013.

leaders.priorTitle: Provost, Vice President for Academic Affairs and Professor of English
leaders.notes: Eleventh president, taking office July 2008 after five years as chief academic officer at Texas A&M International University (a fellow A&M System member), so internal to the A&M System rather than fully external. He died unexpectedly April 29, 2016 at age 63 while still the sitting president; Inside Higher Ed subsequently reported the death was ruled a suicide.

leaders.priorTitle: President
leaders.nextRole: Developmental leave, then returned to the faculty in Literature and Languages (President Emeritus)
leaders.notes: Twelfth president. Named interim president effective June 1, 2016 after Dan Jones's death, moving directly from the TAMIU presidency; the A&M System Board of Regents named him sole finalist in October 2016 and he became permanent president November 10, 2016, so his term was only partly interim. He announced in January 2018 that he would step down effective August 31, 2018, and a search committee was formed in February 2018.

leaders.priorTitle: Vice President for Research and Economic Development
leaders.notes: Thirteenth president and CEO, named sole finalist in July 2018 and appointed by the A&M System Board of Regents August 16, 2018; a genuinely external hire from Boise State, with a Ph.D. in medicinal chemistry from Purdue. He remains in office as of July 2026 with no presidential search under way; the institution was renamed from Texas A&M University-Commerce to East Texas A&M University effective November 2024 during his tenure.

leaders.priorTitle: Vice President for Institutional Advancement
leaders.nextRole: Vice Chancellor for University Advancement (later interim Chancellor)
leaders.notes: President in office during 1996; served 1989 to June 2000, an external hire from Kent State. After EMU he moved to East Carolina University, where he later became interim chancellor.

leaders.priorTitle: President
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Texas at San Antonio
leaders.nextRole: Returned to the American Association of State Colleges and Universities
leaders.nextRoleInstitution: American Association of State Colleges and Universities
leaders.notes: External hire; had been president of the University of Texas at San Antonio in the 1990s and was affiliated with AASCU immediately before EMU. His presidency ended in 2004 amid Board of Regents conflict.

leaders.priorTitle: Executive Vice President
leaders.notes: Internal appointee. Named acting president at the August 2004 Board of Regents meeting for roughly two weeks, bridging Kirkpatrick's departure and interim President Willis's arrival, then became interim provost.

leaders.priorTitle: President (retired), Lock Haven University
leaders.notes: One-year interim appointment effective August 16, 2004 through July 31, 2005. Had been president of Lock Haven University (PA) for 22 years and was credited with restoring campus morale after Kirkpatrick's departure.

leaders.priorTitle: President
leaders.priorInstitution: State University of New York at Potsdam
leaders.nextRole: Associate Vice President for Economic Development and Community Engagement (from 2012)
leaders.notes: External hire from SUNY Potsdam. Fired by the Board of Regents July 15, 2007 over the university's handling and delayed disclosure of the December 2006 rape and murder of student Laura Dickinson (Clery Act violations). He later sued EMU and in 2012 took an administrative post at Ball State University.

leaders.priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs
leaders.nextRole: Returned to Provost, then to School of Social Work faculty
leaders.notes: Internal. Served as senior administrative official/acting head after Fallon's firing until Susan Martin was hired in 2008, then returned to the provostship and later to faculty.

leaders.priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
leaders.nextRole: Sabbatical, then tenured professor of Accounting and Finance
leaders.notes: EMU's 22nd president and its first female president, from the U-M Dearborn provostship. Announced her departure in March 2015 with a final day of July 7, 2015, took a sabbatical, then returned to EMU as a faculty member.

leaders.priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice President of Academic and Student Affairs
leaders.notes: Internal appointee; interim president from July 7, 2015. Departed to become president of Towson University (MD) effective January 2016. (She later moved to the University of Texas at Arlington in 2020, but the role immediately after EMU was the Towson presidency.)

leaders.priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs (retired 2014)
leaders.notes: Came out of retirement for a third stint in the president's office, serving as interim president from December 2015 to June 2016 until James Smith arrived.

leaders.priorTitle: President
leaders.notes: External hire from Northern State University (Aberdeen, SD); began July 1, 2016 and served roughly a decade. He stepped aside at the end of his contract; Kelly began April 1, 2026 ahead of Smith's June 30, 2026 contract conclusion.

leaders.priorTitle: President
leaders.notes: 24th president; a two-time EMU alumnus and Flint native. Elected by the Board of Regents December 10, 2025; joined March 1, 2026 as president-elect and began as president April 1, 2026 on a five-year contract. Earlier roles include president of the University of West Georgia and chancellor of USC Upstate. The presidential search that selected him has concluded.
